prize_parts.citation: For introducing firm heterogeneity into trade theory, showing how selection and reallocation across firms shape who exports and how trade generates gains.

statement.case_for: Melitz (2003), together with the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple work on exports versus FDI, moved the unit of analysis in trade from the country or industry to the firm. It gave a tractable account of exporter selection, within-industry reallocation and a distinct channel for gains from trade. It also links directly to firm-level and transaction-level data, which is the evidence I know best from my own work on pricing, invoicing and exchange-rate pass-through. The framework is more than twenty years old, has been tested on many countries' micro-data, and underlies a large body of quantitative trade-policy analysis. The opening record shows broad cross-field support: nine members place it in their top three and all eleven rank it. I treat that as a signal to examine, not as evidence of merit. The scientific case holds up on its own: the contribution is general, has been confirmed on data, and is clearly attributable to two people.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution and overlap. Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum made closely related empirical and theoretical contributions, and none is credited on this entry. Helpman's earlier monopolistic-competition work is adjacent to Krugman's 2008 prize, so the incremental case for Helpman needs a clear statement. Some welfare conclusions also depend on functional-form assumptions, such as Pareto productivity and CES demand. A committee that held trade to be adequately recognised in 2008 could reasonably prefer a different field.

responses.point: Hassler ranks Kiyotaki-Moore first as the originators of the collateral-constraint amplification mechanism. He limits credit to the two of them because of the 2022 prize, and he notes that Krugman's 2008 prize overlaps with Helpman's earlier contributions.
responses.response: I agree that Kiyotaki-Moore is a clean two-person attribution and a foundational mechanism. I did not rank it in my opening eight, and his argument has moved it to my first alternative. On Krugman, I would answer that Helpman's credit here rests on the heterogeneous-firm extensions, not on the monopolistic-competition base that the 2008 prize covered. Even so, the overlap is real, and it is the main reason the citation should be anchored on selection and reallocation across firms. I still prefer B005 because its confirmation is much more direct. Firm-level data across many countries support the selection and reallocation margins. The collateral channel, as several colleagues note, is harder to identify empirically, and the 2022 overlap makes its marginal case less clear.

responses.point: Dreber-Almenberg ranks B005 fourth. She points out that Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are not among the credited names, so attribution is uncertain, and that Krugman's earlier prize already recognised the new trade theory tradition.
responses.response: The omission is a real attribution problem, and I do not want to play it down. Bernard and Jensen documented the exporter-premium facts that the theory then had to explain. Eaton-Kortum is a Ricardian strand with a different structure. The two-person proposal is therefore not an exhaustive allocation of credit, but I think it is defensible. Melitz supplies the model that unified the facts, and Helpman supplies the broader program, including the export-versus-FDI choice. The citation should name the theoretical integration of firm heterogeneity into trade, not claim the empirical discovery of exporter heterogeneity. I would not extend this to a three-person group. Adding Redding, who ranks fifth for her, would dilute a credit that is cleaner with two names.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B005 second. He treats Melitz (2003) as central and Helpman's broader program as supporting his credit. He sees Redding as an important extender but a less essential third name, and he asks whether Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum should be credited alongside.
responses.response: I share this reading of the three-name question. Redding's quantitative spatial and trade work is important but later and more cumulative, and it may fit better in a separate quantitative-trade entry. I disagree somewhat on the extra names. Widening to Bernard or Eaton-Kortum would turn a clean two-person credit into a contested allocation of a diffuse literature, which creates the same difficulty we face on B019. His point on maturity is the one I weight most. More than two decades of replication separates this from the younger candidates, such as B001 and B026, where long-run confirmation is still accumulating.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the trade field as sufficiently distinct from the 2008 prize, and whether a Melitz-centred credit is cleaner than a Helpman-Melitz pairing.
How to treat Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum, who are not credited on this entry, without an artificial enlargement of the group.

Whether the competing strong candidates, especially B011 and B034, should take precedence. B011 has the most first-place rankings among the openings, but they come mostly from macro-oriented members. My own judgment of the collateral channel's empirical confirmation is based on general knowledge and has not been independently verified.
The three-person limit across the configuration prevents me from combining B005 with a two-person B011 or B034 award, so a single-part configuration is what I can support.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with the credited names on the shortlisted entries is apparent from the supplied profile. For transparency, I disclose three public connections that are not adjudicated. First, my research field (pricing under imperfect competition, exchange-rate pass-through, trade) is adjacent to B005, and my field is also close to the industrial-organisation candidate B034. Second, I have co-authored with committee colleagues John Hassler and Tore Ellingsen (IJIO 2026). Third, I am married to Magdalena Andersson, a Swedish politician, which is noted only as a public fact. I have found no evidence that it bears on this assessment.
